extraction.name: C-EVAL
extraction.description: A Chinese evaluation suite containing 13,948 multiple-choice exam questions across 52 disciplines and four difficulty levels: middle school, high school, college, and professional. Subjects cover STEM, humanities, social science, and other areas. C-EVAL HARD is a subset of eight challenging mathematics, physics, and chemistry subjects designed to assess advanced reasoning abilities.
extraction.creator: Yuzhen Huang, Yuzhuo Bai, Zhihao Zhu, Junlei Zhang, Jinghan Zhang, Tangjun Su, Junteng Liu, Chuancheng Lv, Yikai Zhang, Jiayi Lei, Yao Fu, Maosong Sun, and Junxian He
extraction.citeAs: Yuzhen Huang, Yuzhuo Bai, Zhihao Zhu, Junlei Zhang, Jinghan Zhang, Tangjun Su, Junteng Liu, Chuancheng Lv, Yikai Zhang, Jiayi Lei, Yao Fu, Maosong Sun, and Junxian He. C-EVAL: A Multi-Level Multi-Discipline Chinese Evaluation Suite for Foundation Models. 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023), Track on Datasets and Benchmarks. arXiv:2305.08322v3, 6 November 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors collected multiple-choice questions from real-world Chinese exams at middle school, high school, college, and professional levels. Standard middle and high school subjects were included except English and middle school Chinese. Twenty-five college subjects were selected to cover all 13 official undergraduate major categories, and 12 professional subjects were selected with reference to China's national vocational qualification directory. Questions were sourced primarily from mock exams or small-scale local exams to mitigate pretraining contamination. The authors collected, manually annotated where necessary, and cross-validated the initial data.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The primary sources were mock exams freely available online, mostly in PDF or Microsoft Word documents, with a minor fraction as web pages. Some college-level questions came from past exams at top Chinese universities publicly shared by students. A minor fraction came from national graduate entrance mock exams on the Weipu website (https://kaoyan.cqvip.com/view/postgraduate/index.aspx); authorization was obtained to include around 2,000 of these non-publicly-free questions.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were standardized to exactly four choices: questions with fewer than four options were eliminated, and incorrect options were randomly dropped from questions with more than four. Questions were randomly split within each subject into development, validation, and test sets. Each subject has five development exemplars; the remaining validation and test questions were divided in a 1:9 ratio. The resulting splits contain 260 development, 1,346 validation, and 12,342 test questions. Eight challenging subjects were selected to form C-EVAL HARD.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: PDF documents were converted to text. Questions were parsed into a structured format automatically where possible and manually by the authors otherwise. Complex mathematical notation was manually converted into standard LaTeX. Processing included cleaning, deduplication, fixing typos and incorrect formats from PDF documents, and ensuring LaTeX compiled without syntax errors. Questions underwent several rounds of human validation by the authors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The authors manually annotated questions from PDF or Word documents where necessary and cross-validated the collected data. Each question has four choices and one correct answer. Development exemplars additionally include reasoning explanations. Junlei Zhang prompted GPT-4 using five human-written question-explanation pairs, the question, and its ground-truth answer to generate step-by-step explanations. Yuzhen Huang, Yuzhuo Bai, and Junxian He manually revised the generated explanations to produce the final explanation data.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors cross-validated collected questions and conducted several rounds of human validation. GPT-4-generated development explanations were manually revised before inclusion. No quantitative annotator agreement or disagreement analysis is reported.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to help developers identify strengths and shortcomings of foundation models and foster their development for Chinese users. The authors argue that Chinese-context evaluation should include Chinese culture, history, laws, and competencies relevant to Chinese society rather than simply translating English benchmarks. They also emphasize evaluating models for complex scenarios beyond casual conversation.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Correct-answer options have a slightly uneven distribution: A 22.9%, B 26.0%, C 26.4%, and D 24.7%. The authors describe these fluctuations as relatively small around 25% and similar to MMLU. To investigate model option bias, they evaluated ChatGPT, ChatGLM-6B, and ChatGLM2-6B using five randomly selected distinct option permutations per question and found relatively small variance in overall accuracy.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: C-EVAL does not provide a complete evaluation of LLM abilities. Other abilities, such as reasoning over and calling APIs, and dimensions beyond accuracy, including safety, bias, and robustness, are left for future evaluation. The validation split contains fewer than 30 questions per subject on average, so tracking individual-subject validation accuracy may not yield significant insights. Online exam questions can potentially enter model pretraining data; the authors took measures to mitigate contamination. Five-shot chain-of-thought exemplars can exceed some models' context windows, requiring fewer exemplars for those evaluations.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation and testing of foundation models' advanced knowledge and reasoning in a Chinese context, including zero-shot and few-shot answer-only and chain-of-thought evaluation. Individual subject subsets can assess particular model abilities, and C-EVAL HARD targets advanced reasoning. Development examples support five-shot prompting, with explanations supporting chain-of-thought prompting. The validation split is intended for hyperparameter tuning, and average validation accuracy can serve as an indicator during development. Accuracy is the evaluation metric. Development and validation labels are public; test labels remain private, and users submit predictions to https://cevalbenchmark.com to obtain test accuracy and optionally publish results on the leaderboard. Data and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/hkust-nlp/ceval.
